name: The Black–Scholes Model
statement: A European option’s price can be derived from the underlying asset’s price, strike, volatility, time to expiry, and the risk-free rate.
statementAccent: derived from the underlying asset’s price, strike, volatility, time to expiry, and the risk-free rate
meaning: The Black-Scholes model gives a closed-form formula for pricing European call and put options by assuming the underlying follows geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility and that markets are frictionless and arbitrage-free. It shows an option can be replicated by continuously trading the underlying asset and a risk-free bond, so its price does not depend on the asset’s expected return.
mechanism: The model constructs a riskless, continuously-rebalanced hedge portfolio combining the option and the underlying stock; because this hedge earns the risk-free rate under no-arbitrage, the option’s value must satisfy a partial differential equation — the Black-Scholes PDE — whose closed-form solution is the pricing formula involving the cumulative normal distribution.

examples.text: Fischer Black and Myron Scholes published "The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities" in the Journal of Political Economy in 1973, the same year the Chicago Board Options Exchange opened, and the formula quickly became the market standard.

Myron Scholes and Robert C. Merton, who had extended the derivation, shared the 1997 Nobel Memorial Prize for this methodology; Fischer Black had died in 1995 and was ineligible but credited by the committee.

Scholes and Merton were principals of Long-Term Capital Management, which used such models with leverage around 25-to-1; it lost $4.6 billion in 1998 amid the Russian crisis and needed a $3.65 billion bailout, an episode often cited as showing the model’s real-world limits.

whyItMatters: The formula turned options trading from an ad hoc activity into a standardised, liquid market, enabling the explosive growth of derivatives since the 1970s and giving traders and risk managers a common pricing and hedging language still embedded in modern risk systems.
limits: Its assumptions — constant volatility, no dividends, continuous frictionless trading, lognormal returns — are known to be violated; the "volatility smile" in traded option prices is direct evidence markets do not price options exactly as the model predicts. Warren Buffett has criticised applying it to long-dated options, and some commentators argue model-based derivative pricing contributed to the 2008 crisis.
misreadings: It is sometimes misread as a guarantee of "fair value" rather than a model-dependent approximation; practitioners in fact routinely adjust the volatility input per strike and maturity rather than treating the output as literal truth.
origin: Developed by economists Fischer Black and Myron Scholes, with Robert C. Merton independently extending the proof; published in 1973 in the Journal of Political Economy. Named after Black and Scholes.
